title: When Words Make Puzzles
objective: After this level you can explain the later Wittgenstein's idea that meaning is use and why he thought some philosophical puzzles come from language misfiring.
summary: The later Wittgenstein held that meaning is often use, that ’game’ is joined by family resemblance, and that some puzzles come from language misleading us; Russell was unimpressed.

cards.headline: Try defining “game.” Every definition breaks.
cards.body: Chess, tag, solitaire, catch. Ludwig Wittgenstein thought that your trouble finding the one thing they all share tells you something about meaning, and about philosophy.

cards.headline: Meaning is use
cards.body: Wittgenstein’s Philosophical Investigations was published in 1953, after his death. For a large class of cases, it says, “the meaning of a word is its use in the language.” So don’t hunt for an object the word names, or a feeling in the speaker’s head. Look at what people do with the word.

cards.headline: A toolbox of words
cards.body: “Think of the tools in a tool-box,” he writes: a hammer, pliers, a saw, a screwdriver, a glue-pot. The functions of words are just as varied. And games? Look closely and you find no single feature common to them all, only “a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing.” He called these family resemblances.

cards.headline: When language misfires
cards.body: Wittgenstein thought many philosophical puzzles come from being misled by the surface of words. “I’ll keep it in mind” sounds like “I’ll keep it in this box,” and suddenly the mind looks like a mysterious box with contents. The cure is to recall how we actually use words like mind and memory. Philosophy’s aim, he wrote, is “to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.”

cards.headline: Not everyone was won over
cards.body: His former teacher Bertrand Russell was blunt. In 1959 he wrote that he had not found in the Investigations “anything that seemed to me interesting,” and couldn’t see why a whole school found important wisdom in its pages. Others disagree strongly: Wittgenstein is counted among the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, by some the most important since Kant.

cards.headline: When Words Make Puzzles: the big picture
learned: Meaning is use, in many cases
Words are as varied as tools

questions.prompt: For a large class of cases, what did Wittgenstein say the meaning of a word is?

options.label: The object it names
options.rationale: He tells us not to hunt for that.

options.label: The feeling it causes in the speaker
options.rationale: He tells us not to look there.

options.label: Its entry in a dictionary
options.rationale: He points to what people do with it.

questions.explanation: Philosophical Investigations section 43: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.

questions.prompt: Match each topic with Wittgenstein’s image or name for it.

pairs.right: The way out of the fly-bottle

questions.explanation: Games share only family resemblances, words are like the tools in a tool-box, and philosophy’s aim is to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.

questions.prompt: Plato said many beautiful things share one Form of Beauty. What did Wittgenstein find when he looked at everything called a game?

options.label: One Form of Game that every game shares in
options.rationale: That’s the Platonic picture he rejects.

options.label: A single shared rule that is written into every game ever played
options.rationale: He found no one common feature.

options.label: Overlapping similarities, with no one feature they all share
That the word game has no meaning
options.rationale: It has a meaning: its use.

questions.explanation: Games show family resemblance: a network of overlapping similarities, not one essence like a Platonic Form.
